title: Design principles
purpose: The standing decisions for this project: what it optimises for, what it refuses, and the reasoning behind each. Read this before adding a dependency, a flag, or an abstraction.

goal.statement: Generate video from procedural shaders on machines with no GPU.
goal.motivation: VPS instances, CI runners, containers and cheap cloud tiers frequently have no GPU allocation, or have one that is unavailable to unprivileged processes. A renderer that only needs a C++ compiler and ffmpeg runs anywhere.
goal.non_goal: Real-time interactive preview. Giving that up is what buys everything below.

dependencies.rule: ffmpeg, a C++17 compiler, and the C++ standard library. Nothing else in the render path.
dependencies.rationale: Every added dependency is a machine where this fails to build. The render path is deliberately buildable with a single c++ invocation and no build system at all.
allowed: ffmpeg -- the encoder. Vendored and built from source so the version is pinned.
A C++17 compiler. Only <cmath>, <cstdio>, <vector>, <string>, <thread> are used.
bash for the CLI wrapper -- orchestration only, never in the render path.
python3 standard library for the generator CLI only, which is a development-time convenience and not required to render anything.
forbidden_without_discussion: Any image, math, or vector library. pgl.hpp exists precisely so none is needed.
A build system. If the project needs one, the header layout has gone wrong.
Any package manager or lockfile in the render path.
Third-party python packages, including requests. urllib is in the standard library.

portability: Assume POSIX. Windows support is via WSL, not via ifdefs.
Assume nothing about SIMD width or GPU presence.
Never rely on a math function existing only in one standard library's global namespace; pgl.hpp documents the specific ambiguity trap here.

shader_is_a_pure_function.contract: vec4 mainImage(vec2 FC, const Uniforms& u) must be a pure function of its arguments.
shader_is_a_pure_function.why: Purity is load-bearing, not stylistic. It is what makes three separate features free: row-parallel threading needs no locks; NxN supersampling can call the same function repeatedly; and --at can render frame 900 without rendering the first 899.
consequences: No mutable globals, no static accumulators, no file or clock access.
No rand(). Use the hashes in pnoise.hpp, which are functions of position.
Anything time-dependent must arrive through Uniforms.

stream_do_not_stage.rule: Frames go from the renderer to the encoder through a pipe. Writing them to disk is opt-in.
stream_do_not_stage.why: A 10-second 4K sequence is about 25 GB of uncompressed PPM. Piping makes that 0 bytes, and overlaps encoding with rendering so encode time largely disappears.
stream_do_not_stage.escape_hatch: --frames-dir keeps the numbered frames as well, for re-encoding without re-rendering.

compile_do_not_interpret.rule: A shader is C++ compiled to a native binary, not a script parsed at runtime.
compile_do_not_interpret.why: CPU shading is arithmetic-bound and runs the inner function millions of times per frame. An interpreter loses one to two orders of magnitude. -O3 on real C++ gives autovectorisation and inlining for free.
compile_do_not_interpret.cost: A one to four second compile per shader change, hidden behind a content-addressed cache.
compile_do_not_interpret.accepted_tradeoff: Shaders are trusted code. This project compiles and runs whatever it is pointed at, so a generated shader must be reviewed like any other code before it is run.

architecture.no_hidden_state: Identical arguments produce byte-identical output. Determinism is what makes visual regressions diffable.

cpu_vs_gpu.premise: A CPU renderer is not a degraded GPU. The constraint profile is different, so the idioms should be too.

what_is_lost.throughput: Roughly two to three orders of magnitude fewer shading operations per second.
what_is_lost.screen_space_derivatives: dFdx, dFdy and fwidth cannot exist. A GPU shades in 2x2 quads and subtracts neighbours; a scalar CPU kernel has no neighbours. This is the single biggest porting obstacle and the reason aa.hpp exists.
what_is_lost.texture_units: No free bilinear filtering, mipmapping or wrap modes.

what_is_gained.no_time_budget: Nothing must finish in 16 ms. A frame may take a second. This inverts the usual cost calculus: brute-force supersampling becomes the default antialiasing strategy rather than a luxury.
what_is_gained.unrestricted_control_flow: Deep recursion, early exit, variable-length loops and per-pixel branching cost what they cost, with no warp divergence penalty.
what_is_gained.full_precision_and_debuggability: Doubles are available if needed, and a shader can be run under a debugger, a profiler or a sanitiser like any other program.
what_is_gained.no_driver: No shader compiler bugs, no vendor differences, no context creation. Output is bit-identical across machines of the same architecture.

cpu_vs_gpu.guidance: When porting a GPU shader, spend the budget the GPU could not: raise --samples instead of hand-tuning analytic antialiasing, and raise octave counts instead of faking detail.

cli_philosophy.summary: Small, quiet, composable. See cli-design.json for the specific rules.
principles: One tool per job: ppmr renders, ppm-gen generates. They compose through a file.
Silent on success. Output only what was asked for.
stdout carries data; stderr carries everything else. This is what makes piping possible at all.
Progress only on an interactive terminal.
No versioning, no telemetry, no update checks, no config file until one is actually needed.

visual_principles.note: Defaults that make generated output look deliberate rather than arbitrary. All are overridable; they are starting points, not rules.

items.detail: Accumulated brightness is unbounded. Compress it with tanh() or x/(1+x) so bright regions roll off instead of flat-clipping to white. Clipping is the most reliable tell of an amateur shader.

items.principle: Never let black be pure black
items.detail: Lift the floor by 0.01-0.03. Pure black reads as a hole in the image, and it also hides banding that a slight lift reveals so you can fix it.

items.principle: Aspect-correct by dividing by height, not by resolution
items.detail: p = (FC * 2 - resolution) / resolution.y keeps the vertical range at [-1,1] and lets x extend with aspect. Dividing by resolution stretches the image with the window.

items.principle: Derive colour from phase, not from a palette lookup
items.detail: Offsetting the same expression per channel, or using three phase-shifted cosines, produces continuous in-gamut colour with no table and no interpolation seams.
Smooth edges are cheaper to produce than to repair. Prefer an SDF with analytic coverage, or supersampling, over post-process blurring.

items.principle: Loop seamlessly by making time an angle
items.detail: Drive animation from u.phase * TAU, and give every time-dependent term an integer frequency, so the last frame joins the first exactly. Scrolling or translating cannot loop.
A falloff of about 1 - 0.35 * dot(p,p) focuses attention without reading as a filter.

Converting a vector to an angle with atan and back with cos/sin is usually a sign of an overcomplicated formulation, and trig is comparatively expensive. Rotate with a matrix, compare with a dot product.

review_checklist: Is mainImage still pure? No statics, no rand, no clock.
Does it use u.phase (not u.time) if it is meant to loop?
Are out-of-range colours tonemapped rather than clipped?
Does it divide by resolution.y for aspect correction?
Does it depend on dFdx/fwidth? Those do not exist; use aa.hpp or --samples.
Are magic constants exposed as Param so they can be swept from the CLI?
Does it render correctly at 1 sample, or does it need --samples to look acceptable? Both are valid, but say which.
